messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: planning for completing higher-order derivatives
parts:
On 1/14/14, 11:43 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

> Hi, my favorite parallelism project now is the divide-and-conquer EP idea,
> but it's not quite ready to be implemented.
> I think before doing the stochastic EP that is my dream algorithm, I first want to get the deterministic version
> working, and that will have to wait until our 2nd-derivatives all programmed.

Our current approach to second derivatives work for everything
but the probability functions. So there's no reason not to start
working on projects involving higher-order auto-diff --- you'll just
have to write the log probability function out directly in the Stan
model using log, +, /, *, exp, etc. That's not that hard for the kind
of test problems we want to use to develop max-marginal, VB, or EP.

Michael's devised a new approach to auto-diff that is like Adept's
approach for gradients, but very cleverly generalizes to higher-order
auto-diff. First order will be competitive with or a bit faster
than what we currently do, but higher-order should be much much
faster.

The high-level interfaces through src/stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp are
not going to change, so anything that works with the current system
should work with the new one.

We need to decide whether it's worth getting our current approach
to forward-mode working for probability functions, or just hold
off until we have the new approach working.

The new approach is a lot of work as it requires
all of the special functions in the Stan manual to have all
first (gradient vector), second (Hessian matrix), and third-order (??? tensor)
derivatives worked out analytically, coded, and tested. And we
need to optimize the memory of the basic approach so it's fast.
We can probably get away with just the gradients to start, which
will give us the functionality we currently have exposed to users for
Stan models.

- Bob

On 1/15/14, 2:13 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> We need to decide whether it's worth getting our current approach
>
> to forward-mode working for probability functions, or just hold
> off until we have the new approach working.
>
>
> My horrendously biased vote is to fast track the new approach
> so that we don't have to implement everything twice.

That's also my preference. The only downside is that it'll take
longer than updating what we have now. My first priority there
would be building something that's as efficient as what we have now
for gradients in *both* time and memory usage --- Daniel said he'd
be OK with a 25% slowdown, which I suppose would be OK, my only fear
being that continuing to make this same decision for every general
feature will lead to exponential decay in our speed over time.

Another argument for not worrying about extending what we have now
is that we can still code up models using all the functions, just
not the probability functions.

On the other hand, any testing we'd do now would still be useful going forward,
and all we really have to do is extend OperatorsAndPartials and then
refactor a bit of the insides of each distribution to be more general
(not that this is at all a trivial task).

- Bob
